proposedDescription: Asian drill snail has a thick, ridged shell, commonly about one to two inches long. It lives among shells, gravel and mud around oyster beds, where it bores through the shells of its prey. Small oysters are especially vulnerable, although it also eats other shellfish. Native to the northwestern Pacific, it has traveled with oyster shipments. Clusters of bright yellow, bottle-shaped egg capsules can offer another clue to its presence.

sources.title: Smithsonian NEMESIS: Ocinebrellus inornatus
University of Washington Ruesink Lab: Oyster drills

researchNotes: Directly read Smithsonian's biological synthesis and the University of Washington Ruesink laboratory's original oyster-drill research account. The laboratory describes its own mark-recapture work and feeding observations; it is not a Smithsonian mirror. Smithsonian also cites Ruesink research, so overlapping feeding evidence is acknowledged, while its morphology/range synthesis has additional authors. Omitted disputed introduction dates and universal ecological-impact claims.

proposedDescription: Asian longhorned beetle is a large, glossy black beetle with white spots and long, banded antennae. Its pale larvae feed beneath the bark of hardwood trees, then tunnel deeper into the wood. Maples are among its hosts, and heavy feeding can eventually kill a tree. Round exit holes, chewed egg-laying marks and coarse sawdust-like material are useful signs. Native to Asia, it most likely reached the United States in wood packaging.

Their biological accounts corroborate adult appearance, hardwood hosts, larval tunneling and exit holes. Earlier Massachusetts/Penn State access failures no longer leave the second-source gap. The introduction pathway is phrased as likely, following APHIS; no current quarantine boundary or eradication claim is made.

proposedDescription: Asian marsh snail is a tiny brown snail with a blunt, cone-shaped shell, reaching only about five millimeters. It lives among vegetation high in salt or brackish marshes, where the ground is not continuously underwater. A field study in Japan found it concentrated in middle and upper tidal areas. Native to Japan and Korea, it has also been recorded in Oregon. Smithsonian reports no observed Oregon impacts, which does not establish that impacts are absent.

sources.title: Smithsonian NEMESIS: Assiminea parasitologica

The latter reports field sampling from 2000–2001, published in the 2023 museum bulletin; it supplies independent empirical habitat evidence, not evidence about Oregon. Smithsonian cites earlier regional work, so this is not two independent confirmations of Oregon status. Repeated Oregon report access failures were replaced by the Japanese study. Retained the distinction between impacts unreported and proven absent.

proposedDescription: Asian marshweed looks quite different above and below the water. Its submerged leaves are finely divided and arranged in whorls around the stem; leaves emerging into the air are firmer and toothed. Small pink to violet flowers appear above the surface. This Asian aquatic plant has been sold for aquariums and apparently escaped cultivation in the southeastern United States. Some stem fragments can root and regrow, while dense stands can shade and crowd other aquatic plants.

sources.title: University of Florida IFAS: Limnophila sessiliflora
California Department of Food and Agriculture (2024): Limnophila sessiliflora Pest Rating Proposal

researchNotes: Read UF's full account and CDFA's June 2024 Pest Rating Proposal. CDFA independently supplies detailed morphology through Flora of North America, Flora of China, Philcox and Yang/Yen, rather than simply reproducing UF; aquarium-trade and some impact passages do cite UF and are not counted as independent confirmation. CDFA reports a fragment experiment with limited regeneration and a minimum fragment size, so prose says some fragments, not every fragment. Flora of China, NTU and other access alternatives failed before the CDFA source succeeded.

Fragment regeneration and dense growth affecting other vegetation.

proposedDescription: Asian ponysfoot forms a low green carpet of small, rounded to kidney-shaped leaves. Its creeping stems root as they spread, while tiny greenish-white flowers sit close to the ground and are easy to miss. Fine hairs, especially beneath the leaves, help with identification. It has been grown as a lawn substitute and can occur among lawn grasses. Related Dichondra species look similar, and regional references warn that this scientific name has sometimes been applied inconsistently.

sources.title: New Zealand Plant Conservation Network: Dichondra micrantha

proposedDescription: Asian shore crab has a square shell with three small teeth along each front side. Lifted rocks in the intertidal zone reveal the sheltered spaces it uses between tides. It eats both plant material and small animals, including shellfish. Native to the western Pacific, it has established along parts of the eastern United States. Some invaded rocky shores support dense populations, where its feeding and competition can affect other members of the shore community.

sources.title: Smithsonian NEMESIS: Hemigrapsus sanguineus

Effects in the description come from Smithsonian's reviewed Atlantic studies and are geographically qualified.

proposedDescription: Asian spiderflower is a sticky, hairy annual with bright yellow flowers and leaves usually divided into five leaflets, though some have three. The slender stems can reach about three feet, with long, narrow seed pods developing among the upper leaves. Glandular hairs give the plant its noticeably sticky surface and help distinguish it from other yellow-flowered herbs. Older botanical accounts call it Cleome viscosa; this catalog retains Arivela viscosa for the same species.

No location-specific invasive impact is claimed; that would require a separate regional assessment, not a description-only inference.

proposedDescription: Asian swamp eels historically grouped as Monopterus albus have long, smooth, scaleless bodies, small eyes and greatly reduced fins. They breathe air and shelter in muddy wetlands, ponds and slow-moving waters, feeding on small aquatic animals. Research has revealed several genetically distinct forms within this group. This overview describes their shared biology; it does not establish the identity of individual U.S. populations. Florida records now assigned to M. javanensis should not automatically be attributed to M. albus.

sources.title: US Fish and Wildlife Service (2025): Asian Swamp Eel ecological risk screening summary
Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission: Swamp Eels

Matsumoto et al. (2010): Cryptic diversification of the swamp eel Monopterus albus in East and Southeast Asia
Damsgaard et al. (2014): High blood oxygen affinity in the air-breathing swamp eel Monopterus albus

researchNotes: Scope-limited descriptive gap resolved, not occurrence identity. In addition to the directly read FWS synthesis, FWC field-program account and Britz/Kottelat nomenclatural paper, directly read substantive abstracts of two original independent studies: Matsumoto et al. analyzed 84 specimens from 13 Asian localities and found distinct genetic clades; Damsgaard et al. experimentally measured blood oxygen-binding physiology in fish published as M. albus. Their independently generated genetic and physiological evidence supports a historical-species-complex overview, without assuming those research specimens represent M. albus sensu stricto. FWS supplies shared external morphology, habitat and diet; its citation of Matsumoto is acknowledged rather than counted as a second genetic observation. FWC assigns Florida populations to M. javanensis and Ophichthys cuchia. No Florida impact, national establishment claim or automatic synonym merge is proposed. The retained catalog ID is unchanged; specimen/occurrence assignments and any final ICZN ruling remain unverified and require separate taxonomic work. The profile explicitly states this scope, so occurrence uncertainty alone no longer blocks a conservative biological description.

proposedDescription: Asian waterwort is a tiny, creeping herb of wet mud and shallow water. Its delicate, branching stems carry small leaves and can produce roots at the joints, helping it spread over damp ground. Field observations describe it in rice fields, irrigation channels and other persistently wet cultivated places. It closely resembles other waterworts, especially Elatine triandra. The stalks beneath its flowers and fruits, together with other small botanical details, are more reliable identification clues than its low-growing shape alone.

Earlier IISc text and failed FNA access are replaced by these directly read sources. Local Niger crop effects are not generalized to US ecological impact.

proposedDescription: Asiatic clam has a rounded, roughly triangular shell marked by strong concentric ridges, usually yellowish to brown. It filters tiny particles from freshwater and can also feed on organic material in the sediment. Rapid growth and reproduction can build dense populations that alter food and nutrient conditions. Large numbers may clog water intakes. Effects on native mussels vary among places, so the presence of this clam alone does not establish why a native population has declined.

sources.title: Smithsonian NEMESIS: Corbicula fluminea

Smithsonian uses C. fluminea provisionally for certain invasive lineages and says native-mussel effects vary. Retained catalog identity but softened universal competition language and did not resolve lineages by shell appearance alone.

proposedDescription: Asiatic dock has large lower leaves and upright flowering stems that rise above the surrounding vegetation. It grows along rivers, in meadows and in disturbed ground, where seeds and spreading underground stems can help it form patches. Research in Central Europe found that light and shallow burial strongly influenced seedling emergence, helping explain establishment in gaps and disturbed soil. It has expanded in parts of Europe, but those regional findings do not establish its effects in every place it occurs.

sources.title: USDA APHIS: Weed risk assessment for Rumex confertus

APHIS and the paper share some background literature, but the authors' light, salinity and burial experiments supply independent primary biological evidence. Sources differ in labeling the life cycle perennial versus biennial; omitted that label rather than silently choosing. European spread is geographically bounded and no US impact claim is inferred.

proposedDescription: Asparagus fern is a flowering plant with fine, feathery-looking growth. The narrow green structures that resemble leaves are modified stems; its true leaves are much smaller. True Asparagus densiflorus has upright, closely branched growth, with small white to pinkish flowers that can develop into red berries. It grows naturally on sandy ground in southeastern Africa. Garden names are often mixed with Asparagus aethiopicus, so an arching plant sold as a Sprengeri asparagus fern may represent that related species instead.

Wisconsin conflates names/cultivars, so only shared modified-stem, flower and berry biology is used from it, not Sprengeri identity, sexual system or invasion status. SANBI attempts remained blocked. Replaced the mixed upright-to-arching description with the accepted botanical concept; existing catalog ID is retained.

proposedDescription: Aspen leafblotch miner spends its larval life inside the leaves of aspens and cottonwoods. Young larvae feed on sap, while later stages remove internal leaf tissue and leave a visible blotch. Silk can draw the mined area into a raised fold. The insect also pupates within its mine before emerging as a tiny moth. These altered patches on leaves are often easier to notice than the adults; a leaf mine still needs careful identification because other insects make similar marks.

The Turkish study reports one generation whereas other regions may have more; no universal generation count was added. MassMoths was also read but is unnecessary to meet the two-source threshold. No non-native or invasive designation is inferred from plant feeding.

Tiny adult moths.

Pupation within leaf mine and subsequent adult emergence.

proposedDescription: Asthmaweed develops upright, leafy stems carrying many tiny flower heads in a broad, branching cluster. Narrow leaves and the nearly hairless bracts around the heads help distinguish this species from some similar fleabanes. Its small fruits carry fine, pale bristles. It grows in disturbed places, including roadsides and river margins. Modern treatments place Conyza floribunda in Erigeron as Erigeron floribundus; older records sometimes mix it with E. sumatrensis, so those records need a name check.

proposedDescription: Australian fingergrass is easiest to recognize by its little windmill-shaped seed heads. Usually six to nine slender branches spread almost horizontally from the top of a stem, with the florets turning dark as they mature. Narrow leaves form a low, dense clump beneath flowering stems that can reach about knee height. Native to Australia, it grows on varied soils and flowers in response to rain. The detached seed heads can tumble in the wind, helping scatter seed.

proposedDescription: Australian tortoise beetle is a rounded brown beetle, often mottled with darker marks, that feeds on eucalyptus. Adults and larvae chew the leaves, leaving curved or semicircular notches along the edges. Adults commonly feed at night and shelter beneath loose bark during the day, a habit also documented in Chilean field collections. Introduced populations occur in California. Established, well-cared-for trees often tolerate feeding, although heavy defoliation can add stress; finding beetles does not by itself show how seriously a tree is affected.

California damage severity and tree tolerance are supported by UC, not extrapolated from the Chilean collection. Retained that established trees often tolerate feeding, not a guarantee of harmlessness.

proposedDescription: Australian tubeworm lives inside a hard, pale tube attached to a submerged surface. A feathery crown reaches into the water to collect tiny food particles, then withdraws into the tube when disturbed. It favors sheltered brackish places such as estuaries, lagoons and docks. Many generations can build tangled, reef-like colonies, although reefs do not form everywhere it occurs. It also grows on boat hulls and structures. Despite its common name, an Australian native origin remains uncertain.

Warm shallow/brackish estuaries, docks and lagoons; hulls and pipes as substrates.

proposedDescription: Australian waterbuttons is a small, low-growing plant with finely divided leaves and tiny flower heads that look like buttons. The heads are cream to pale yellow and lack the showy outer petals of many daisies. Slender stems may lie along the ground or turn upward, and can root where they touch suitable soil. Look for it in lawns, roadsides, open grassland and other disturbed places. Its modest size can make the button heads easier to notice than the plant beneath them.
